name: Cryogenic Cost and Scale
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: There Is No Bigger Fridge
lesson.summary: Dilution refrigerators are expensive, physically large, and have a coldest stage with only microwatts of cooling power to spare, which imposes a real physical ceiling on how much hardware can be packed in, not just a cost problem.
lesson.body:
A dilution refrigerator capable of reaching the millikelvin temperatures a superconducting quantum chip needs is not a small or cheap piece of equipment. These systems are typically arranged as a series of nested, gold-plated cooling stages, often described informally as looking like an inverted metal chandelier, housed inside a vacuum chamber roughly the size of a large closet or small room. A single research-grade dilution refrigerator system commonly costs several hundred thousand to well over a million dollars, takes on the order of a day or more just to cool down from room temperature to its base operating point, and needs specialized cryogenic engineering expertise to install, maintain, and troubleshoot.

The scaling problem is not simply that fridges are expensive, it is that the coldest stage, the part actually holding the qubit chip, has severely limited cooling power by design. At millikelvin temperatures, a dilution refrigerator's coldest stage can typically remove only a few microwatts of heat, an extraordinarily small budget. Every wire, every component, and every bit of stray electromagnetic energy that reaches that stage draws against this tiny cooling budget, which directly limits how much hardware, and by extension how many qubits and their associated wiring, can physically be crammed into that coldest region without warming it beyond its useful operating range.

This creates a genuine physical ceiling, not just a cost problem. You cannot simply build a much larger dilution refrigerator and expect the coldest stage's cooling power to scale proportionally, because the engineering of reaching millikelvin temperatures gets harder, not easier, as the cooled volume and the amount of wiring and material inside it grows. Nobody has yet built or demonstrated a dilution refrigerator system capable of hosting the wiring and control hardware for a million qubits at the coldest stage using current cryostat designs. Current research into this problem includes larger custom cryostats, splitting qubits across multiple linked refrigerators, and moving as much control electronics as possible to warmer stages of the fridge, or out of it entirely, to reduce what the coldest stage has to support.

This is why cryogenic cost and scale sits at the center of the hardware scaling wall discussed later in this chapter. It is not just that refrigeration is expensive today and might get cheaper with investment, the way other technologies have. It is that the specific physics of extracting heat at millikelvin temperatures imposes a cooling-power budget that current cryostat designs cannot stretch arbitrarily far, no matter how much money is spent on a bigger version of the same basic design.

Multiple refrigerators can in principle be linked together, and this is one of the directions the field is actively pursuing, but it trades one hard problem for another. Connecting qubits across separate refrigerators requires some kind of reliable link, whether microwave, optical, or otherwise, between systems that are each independently cooled, wired, and controlled, and building low-loss connections between physically separate cold environments is itself an open area of research rather than an off-the-shelf solution.
